title: Task 1: Line graph
summary: Describe how one or more values change over time: rises, falls, fluctuations, peaks and points where lines cross.
rule: Overview = main trends with NO numbers; bodies = key figures, not every year.

do: 0–3 min: find trends, highs, lows, crossings
Intro: paraphrase the task in 1 sentence
'Overall,' + main trends, no numbers
2 bodies: start, changes, end values; compare
avoid: Numbers or years in the overview
No overview → Task Achievement capped at 5
Describing every year instead of key points

steps: Minutes 0-3: read the task, the title, axes, units and legend; find the main trends, the highest/lowest values and any crossings; decide how to split the data into two body groups.
Introduction (1 sentence, ~25 words): paraphrase - The line graph illustrates / presents data on + what + where + over the period from X to Y. Name the lines with 'namely' if there are few.

Overview (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): 'Overall,' + the general trend of each group (up / down) contrasted with while / whereas + the biggest change or the change of leader (e.g. 'China surpassed it and ranked first'). No numbers.
Body 1 (~60 words): the lines that started highest or fell - start value with year, main changes, end value.
Body 2 (~60 words): the lines that rose or started lowest - start value, changes, end value, crossings and peaks; compare with Body 1 lines (By comparison, / By contrast,).
Use both sentence patterns (rose sharply / there was a sharp rise) and approximations (around, just over, nearly).
Minutes 17-20: check numbers against the chart, units (thousands / millions / %), tenses, the/a, subject-verb agreement and the word count (at least 150; aim 170-190).
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Under 150 words, or spending more than 20 minutes and losing time for Task 2 (which counts double).
Describing every single point year by year instead of selecting start, end, peaks, lows and crossings.
Wrong tense with 'by': By 2012 they HAD surged ... (past perfect), not 'surged'.
Wrong preposition: rose TO 10% (new level) vs rose BY 2% (size of change); peaked AT; a peak OF.
Using 'the number of' with uncountable nouns (the amount of money, not the number of money).
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction (1 sentence), Overview (1-2 sentences, 'Overall,'), Body 1, Body 2. No conclusion is needed - the overview does that job.
Approximate word targets: introduction ~25-30, overview ~35-45, each body paragraph ~55-70 words.
Vary the subject: the number of / the figure for / that of / this figure - don't repeat the same noun.
Group lines with similar trends together (falling lines in Body 1, rising lines in Body 2), or the highest lines first.
If the graph has projected years (2030, 2040), use the prediction structures (is expected to, is predicted to, it is estimated that) and mention the projection in the overview.
Point out crossings and changes of rank: overtook, surpassed, outnumbered, became the largest.
example: Australian exports (1990-2012): Overview - 'an upward trend was seen in ... India and China, while the US and Japan witnessed an opposite trend ... at the beginning Japan was the main importer ..., whereas in the last year China surpassed it and ranked first.' Body 1 = Japan (highest, falling) + US (fluctuating); Body 2 = China (lowest to highest) + India (steady rise).

title: Task 1: Bar chart
summary: Compare categories shown as bars - either over several years (dynamic: trend language) or at one point in time (static: comparison and ranking language).
rule: Several years = trend language; one year only = compare and rank.

do: 0–3 min: several years or one? Find highs, lows
Intro: paraphrase what, where, when
'Overall,' + main trend or ranking, no numbers
2 bodies with direct comparisons
avoid: Numbers or years in the overview
Trend verbs (rose, fell) for a one-year chart
Misreading units (thousands of dollars)

steps: Minutes 0-3: read the task, the title, axes, units and legend; find the main trends, the highest/lowest values and any crossings; decide how to split the data into two body groups. Decide first: are there several years (dynamic) or one year (static)?
Introduction (1 sentence, ~25 words): The bar chart illustrates / compares + what + where + when (over a twelve-year period from 2006 to 2018 / in 2004).
Overview (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): 'Overall,' + the main trend (dynamic) or main comparison (static) + the highest category and any change of ranking. No numbers.
Body 1 (~60 words): dynamic - the categories with steadier or mixed changes; static - the first group (e.g. doctors), from highest to lowest.
Body 2 (~60 words): dynamic - the category with the most dramatic change; static - the second group (e.g. other workers), with direct comparisons (... which was $10,000 less than Italy).
Minutes 17-20: check numbers against the chart, units (thousands / millions / %), tenses, the/a, subject-verb agreement and the word count (at least 150; aim 170-190).
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Under 150 words, or spending more than 20 minutes and losing time for Task 2 (which counts double).
Using trend verbs (rose, fell) for a static chart with only one year - there is no change over time; compare instead.
Misreading the units: 'thousands of US dollars' means 120 on the axis = $120,000.
Listing every bar in order without comparisons.
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction (1 sentence), Overview (1-2 sentences, 'Overall,'), Body 1, Body 2. No conclusion is needed - the overview does that job.
Approximate word targets: introduction ~25-30, overview ~35-45, each body paragraph ~55-70 words.
Vary the subject: the number of / the figure for / that of / this figure - don't repeat the same noun.
Static ranking language: topped the list, led with a substantial advantage, held the top spot, the joint second-place holders, recorded the lowest, respectively, the remaining three countries.
Dynamic language: stood at, before rising significantly to, saw a decline to, exhibited a steady upward trend, culminating in, surpassed.
example: Annual pay of doctors and other workers in 2004 (static): Overview - 'physicians consistently commanded higher salaries than other professionals in all countries surveyed. The United States topped the list for both ...' Body 1 = doctors (from $120,000 in the US to $50,000 in Finland); Body 2 = other workers.

title: Task 1: Pie chart
summary: Describe proportions of a whole (100%): the largest and smallest segments, and changes between years if there are several pies.
rule: Show the biggest and smallest shares; group the small segments together.

do: 0–3 min: one year (rank) or several (changes)?
Intro: the proportion of… + who + when
'Overall,' + largest / smallest share, no numbers
Body 1: largest shares; Body 2: the rest
avoid: Numbers or percentages in the overview
'Percentage' in every sentence: vary it
9% → 16% = 7 percentage points, not 7%

steps: Minutes 0-3: read the task, the title, axes, units and legend; find the main trends, the highest/lowest values and any crossings; decide how to split the data into two body groups. Note whether the pies show different years (describe changes) or one year (rank the segments).
Introduction (1 sentence, ~25 words): The pie chart(s) illustrate(s) the percentage / proportion of ... + who/what + when.

Overview (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): 'Overall,' + the largest (and smallest) segment; with several years add the main changes / change of leader (were overtaken by buses as the primary choice). No numbers.
Body 1 (~60 words): the largest segments with figures and comparisons (accounted for over half, at 51%; nearly twice as much as).
Body 2 (~60 words): 'Regarding the remaining categories,' - the smaller segments, ending with the smallest (a mere 3%, less than 1%).
Minutes 17-20: check numbers against the chart, units (thousands / millions / %), tenses, the/a, subject-verb agreement and the word count (at least 150; aim 170-190).
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Under 150 words, or spending more than 20 minutes and losing time for Task 2 (which counts double).
Repeating 'percentage' in every sentence - rotate proportion / share / figure / fractions (just over a quarter, roughly three quarters).
Describing each of many small segments separately - group the small ones together.
Writing 'rose by 7%' when you mean percentage points (9% -> 16% is a rise of seven percentage points).
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction (1 sentence), Overview (1-2 sentences, 'Overall,'), Body 1, Body 2. No conclusion is needed - the overview does that job.
Approximate word targets: introduction ~25-30, overview ~35-45, each body paragraph ~55-70 words.
Vary the subject: the number of / the figure for / that of / this figure - don't repeat the same noun.
Use the share verbs: account for, constitute, comprise, make up, represent, hold the largest share.
With two years, give both values in each sentence: rising from 9% to 16% between 2004 and 2009.
example: Transport to a university, 2004 vs 2009: Overview - 'private cars were the most popular means of transport at the beginning of the period, while they were overtaken by buses as the primary choice in the final year.' Body 1 = cars and buses (the two that swapped places); Body 2 = bicycle, walking, train.

title: Task 1: Table
summary: Select the key figures from many exact numbers: highest and lowest values, the biggest gaps and the patterns across rows and columns.
rule: Select the key figures (highest, lowest, biggest gaps); don't copy the table.

do: 0–3 min: mark the biggest and smallest numbers
Intro: paraphrase what, who, when
'Overall,' + patterns across rows and columns
2 bodies, with a comparison in every sentence
avoid: Numbers in the overview
Turning the whole table into sentences
Treating a table with years as static

steps: Minutes 0-3: read the task, the title, axes, units and legend; find the main trends, the highest/lowest values and any crossings; decide how to split the data into two body groups. Mark the largest and smallest numbers; compare rows (e.g. age groups) and columns (e.g. male vs female); if there are years, note the direction of each row.
Introduction (1 sentence, ~25 words): The table illustrates / shows the percentage(s) of ... + who + when (+ classified by gender / by region).
Overview (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): 'Overall,' + the main pattern across rows + the main pattern across columns, or the highest/lowest category at the end. No numbers.
Body 1 (~60 words): the first group of rows/columns with figures and direct comparisons (compared with a slightly higher figure of ...; whereas the corresponding figure for ...).
Body 2 (~60 words): the remaining rows/columns ('When it comes to ...', 'In terms of ...').
Minutes 17-20: check numbers against the chart, units (thousands / millions / %), tenses, the/a, subject-verb agreement and the word count (at least 150; aim 170-190).
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Under 150 words, or spending more than 20 minutes and losing time for Task 2 (which counts double).
Copying the whole table into sentences - select only the main features.
Treating a table with years as static - if there are years, describe it like a line graph with trend verbs.
Confusing % with percentage points when describing differences between two percentages.
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction (1 sentence), Overview (1-2 sentences, 'Overall,'), Body 1, Body 2. No conclusion is needed - the overview does that job.
Approximate word targets: introduction ~25-30, overview ~35-45, each body paragraph ~55-70 words.
Vary the subject: the number of / the figure for / that of / this figure - don't repeat the same noun.
Compare in every sentence: compared with, whereas the corresponding figure for, a similar pattern was observed among.
Use 'making this group the least active overall' / 'making it the highest initial share' to add a ranking comment.
example: Cycling by age and gender in 2011: Overview - younger people cycled more, and females cycled more than males in every age group, with the biggest gap among teenagers. Body 1 = the three youngest groups (male vs female in each); Body 2 = 40-59 and 60+.
language: A similar pattern was observed among

title: Task 1: Map
summary: Describe changes to a place over time, or compare possible sites, using location language and mostly passive verbs - there are no numbers.
rule: Say what was added, removed or changed; use the passive; no numbers.

do: 0–3 min: list added, removed, unchanged features
Intro: the maps illustrate the changes in…
Overview: the biggest change, no years
2 bodies by area or by time, in the passive
avoid: Active verbs ('the school built')
'in the north of' (inside) vs 'to the north of'
Forgetting what stayed the same
remember: Then vs now: present perfect passive

steps: Minutes 0-3: compare the maps; list what was added, removed, replaced, extended and what stayed the same; note the dates and the compass directions. Decide whether to organise the body by area (north/south) or by time (1960-1980 / 2000).

Introduction (1 sentence, ~25-30 words): The provided map(s) illustrate(s) the structural changes and developments that occurred at / in ... between ... and ... (two sites: illustrates two proposed locations for ...).
Overview (1-2 sentences, ~35-45 words): the most significant change without data or years - did the area become more urbanized, commercialized, industrialized or accessible? What stayed the same?
Body 1 (~65 words): the first area (e.g. the northern sector) or time period, or site 1 - location + changes in the passive (was replaced by, was converted into, was demolished).
Body 2 (~65 words): the second area / period / site, with linking (Conversely, / Meanwhile, / By the year 2000, further redevelopments took place).
Minutes 17-20: check tenses (past simple passive; present perfect passive for 'today'; had + V3 with 'by'), prepositions (in the north of vs to the north of) and the word count.
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Using active verbs as if buildings acted by themselves ('the school built') - use the passive (a school was built).
Mixing up 'in the north of' (inside the area) and 'to the north of' (outside it).
Forgetting features that did NOT change - saying what remained unchanged is part of the comparison.
Wrong tense for a 'then and now' map: use the present perfect passive (has been cleared, has been constructed).
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction, Overview, 1st main feature, 2nd main feature (teacher's 'The Structure of MAP').
Ready-made overview types: urbanization, commercialization/leisure, industrialization, infrastructure/accessibility, internal layout changes.
For two possible sites use the present simple (S1 is situated ..., whereas S2 is centrally located ...) and compare their advantages.
Planned future changes: is planned to be built / it is planned that ... will.
example: Queen Mary Hospital 1960-1980-2000: Overview - the whole area underwent significant modernization; medical facilities expanded while green space and parking shrank. Body 1 = 1960 and the changes by 1980 (shopping center replaced by a Cancer Centre; farmland cleared for a Nursing School); Body 2 = 2000 (Cancer Centre tripled in size; Nursing School relocated, halving the car park).
language: was cleared to make way for

title: Task 1: Process diagram
summary: Describe every stage of a man-made or natural process in order, using sequence linkers and the present simple passive.
rule: Describe every stage in order, using the passive and sequence words.

do: 0–3 min: count the stages, find first and last
Intro: the diagram illustrates the process of…
Overview: X stages, beginning with… ending in…
Body 1: first half; Body 2: second half
avoid: Skipping a stage
then… then… then: vary the sequencers
Active voice for a man-made process
remember: Man-made = passive; natural cycle = often active

steps: Minutes 0-3: count the stages, find the first and last stage, note whether the process is man-made (passive) or natural / a cycle (often active), and underline the label nouns you must use (kiln, mould, turbine).
Introduction (1 sentence, ~20-25 words): The diagram illustrates the step-by-step process of ... / The process diagram illustrates the generation of ...
Overview (1-2 sentences, ~30-40 words): 'Overall, there are (7) stages in the process, beginning with ___ and culminating in ___.' (+ simple / complex; two diagrams: compare their complexity).
Body 1 (~60-70 words): the first half of the stages, in order, with varied sequencers (Initially, / The process starts when ... / Next, / After that,).
Body 2 (~60-70 words): the second half of the stages (Subsequently, / Once this stage is complete, / Finally,), or the second diagram if there are two.
Minutes 17-20: check that no stage is missing, that the passive is correct (is dug, are fired) and the word count.
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Skipping a stage - every stage must be mentioned, in order (e.g. the drying oven stage in the brick process).
Repeating 'then ... then ... then' - vary the sequencers.
Active voice for man-made processes ('workers dig the clay') - use the passive (clay is dug).
Ignoring the labels and numbers on the diagram (temperatures, times) - include them in the body.
tips: Raise the grammar score with -ing and relative clauses: after being crushed, before being purified, resulting in, which / where / in which.
Useful whole-process language: the process consists of (5) stages, this is done by machine, production is largely mechanised, the final product, ready for distribution.
Natural cycles end with something like 'allowing the process to continue / the cycle begins again'.
example: Brick manufacturing: Overview - 'the production involves nine key stages, beginning with raw material extraction and culminating in delivery.' Body 1 = digging, grid and roller, adding sand and water, moulding / wire cutting, drying; Body 2 = two kiln firings, cooling chamber, packaging and delivery.
language: is heated / is filtered / are packaged

title: Task 1: Multiple / mixed graphs
summary: Two different visuals on one topic (e.g. line graph + bar chart, pie chart + table): select the key feature of each and describe them in separate paragraphs.
rule: One body paragraph per visual; the overview covers both.

do: 0–3 min: find the main feature of each visual
Intro: paraphrase both, joined with 'while'
'Overall,' + key feature of each, no numbers
Body 1 = graph 1 only; Body 2 = graph 2 only
avoid: Mixing both charts in one paragraph
An overview about only one chart
Trying to describe everything in both

steps: Minutes 0-3: study both visuals, find the main feature of each (trend, max/min) and any obvious link between them.
Introduction (1 sentence, ~30 words): paraphrase both tasks joined with while / and (The line graph shows ..., while the bar chart shows ...).
Overview (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): 'Overall,' + the key feature of graph 1 + the key feature of graph 2 (increase/decrease, max/min). No numbers.
Body 1 (~60-70 words): the first graph only.
Body 2 (~60-70 words): the second graph only (Looking at ... / In terms of ... / Turning to ...).
Minutes 17-20: check numbers against the chart, units (thousands / millions / %), tenses, the/a, subject-verb agreement and the word count (at least 150; aim 170-190).
traps: Numbers, percentages or years in the overview - the teacher's rule is NO NUMBER/PERCENTAGE/YEAR there.
No overview at all, or an overview that only lists categories - this caps Task Achievement at band 5.
Copying the question word for word in the introduction instead of paraphrasing.
Giving opinions or reasons that the chart does not show (Task 1 is a report).
Under 150 words, or spending more than 20 minutes and losing time for Task 2 (which counts double).
Mixing data from both charts in the same paragraph - keep one paragraph per visual.
An overview that covers only one of the charts.
Trying to describe everything in both charts - with 20 minutes you must select.
tips: Approximate word targets: introduction ~25-30, overview ~35-45, each body paragraph ~55-70 words.
Vary the subject: the number of / the figure for / that of / this figure - don't repeat the same noun.

Structure (teacher's board notes): INTRODUCTION - paraphrase the tasks, while/and; OVERVIEW - Overall, no number/percentage/year, increase/decrease, max/min; DETAIL PART - the first graph, the second graph.
Use the language of each chart type: trend language for the line graph, share language for the pie chart, comparison/ranking for a static bar chart or table.
example: Visits to and from the UK (line) + top destinations in 1999 (bar): Overview - both numbers increased and residents going abroad always outnumbered visitors; France and Spain were the most popular destinations. Body 1 = line graph (start and end values); Body 2 = bar chart from most to least popular.

title: Task 2: Opinion (agree / disagree)
summary: Give your opinion on ONE statement ('Do you agree or disagree?' / 'To what extent do you agree or disagree?') and support it with two reasons.
rule: Pick one side and keep the same opinion from introduction to conclusion.

do: 0–5 min: underline every part, plan 2 reasons
Intro: paraphrase + your opinion + 2 reasons
Bodies: one reason each + a named example
Conclusion: restate opinion, no new ideas
avoid: An unclear or changing position
No named example (country, study, WHO)
Writing both sides as in a discussion essay

steps: Minutes 0-5: read the instruction line and identify the essay type; underline every part of the question; choose your position (if needed) and plan two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, explanation, result and a named real-world example.

Introduction (2-3 sentences, ~50 words): paraphrase the question, give your opinion and state your two supporting reasons (I disagree with the idea that ..., because ...). An optional concession first: While ... is definitely important, ...
Body 1 (~110 words): topic sentence with your 1st reason (To begin with, ...), explanation, result, example (A great example of this is seen in ...).
Body 2 (~110 words): topic sentence with your 2nd reason (Furthermore, / Similarly, ...), explanation, result, example (For instance, a recent study by ... confirmed that ...).
Conclusion (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): In conclusion, while ..., I strongly believe that ... + the two reasons in new words.

Minutes 35-40: check that every part of the question is answered, your position is the same in the introduction and conclusion, and check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, plurals, spelling of topic words and the word count (250+; aim 280-320).
traps: Under 250 words - the teacher's models are 300-350 words; aim for about 280-320.
Body paragraphs with no named example ('some countries') - name a country, organisation or study (WHO, Harvard, Finland).
Introducing new ideas in the conclusion.
Memorised, off-topic sentences or copying the question - paraphrase the topic with synonyms.
Starting every sentence with a linking word, or using 'On the other hand' just to add a point.
An unclear or changing position - the same opinion must appear in the introduction, both topic sentences and the conclusion.
Writing a discussion essay (one paragraph per side) when the question only asks for your opinion.
Two thin reasons in one paragraph instead of one well-developed reason per paragraph.
For 'To what extent ...' not saying how far you agree (completely / partly).
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction (2-3 sentences), Body 1 (5-6 sentences), Body 2 (5-6 sentences), Conclusion (1-2 sentences).
Approximate word targets: introduction ~45-55, each body paragraph ~100-120, conclusion ~35-45 words.
Task 2 counts about twice as much as Task 1 - never run out of time for it (spend 40 minutes).
Use topic vocabulary from the matching 'Writing Topic' set in the vocabulary trainer (4-5 phrases per essay).
Both body paragraphs support YOUR side; deal with the other side in one 'While ...' clause in the introduction or conclusion.
Give the two reasons in the thesis in the same order as the body paragraphs.
example: 'A big salary is more important than job satisfaction.' Thesis: I disagree ... because long-term happiness and health depend on job satisfaction. Body 1 = mental health (Doctors Without Borders); Body 2 = happy workers are more productive and get promoted (Gallup: 21% more profitable).
language: I disagree with the idea that
I completely agree with this perspective
In conclusion, while ..., I strongly believe that

title: Task 2: Discussion (discuss both views + opinion)
summary: Discuss two opposing views fairly AND say which one you support.
rule: Present both views fairly, then clearly say which one you support.

do: 0–5 min: plan; the view you agree with = Body 2
Intro: both views + your opinion
Body 1: the view you disagree with, fairly
Body 2: your view + example; then conclude
avoid: Forgetting your own opinion
Attacking the first view inside Body 1
Unbalanced paragraphs (one long, one short)

steps: Minutes 0-5: read the instruction line and identify the essay type; underline every part of the question; choose your position (if needed) and plan two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, explanation, result and a named real-world example. Decide which view you agree with - it goes in Body 2.
Introduction (2-3 sentences, ~55 words): introduce both views (It is often argued that ..., whereas others contend that ...) and state your opinion (While ..., I believe that ... due to / by ...).
Body 1 (~110 words): the view you DISAGREE with - On the one hand, many people believe that ... ; explain why people hold it (Proponents of this view maintain that ...); example.
Body 2 (~110 words): the view you AGREE with - On the other hand, I agree with the perspective that ... ; explain why it is stronger; example (For instance, ...).
Conclusion (1-2 sentences, ~45 words): In conclusion, although ..., ... . Ultimately, I maintain that ... because ...

Minutes 35-40: check that every part of the question is answered, your position is the same in the introduction and conclusion, and check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, plurals, spelling of topic words and the word count (250+; aim 280-320).
traps: Under 250 words - the teacher's models are 300-350 words; aim for about 280-320.
Body paragraphs with no named example ('some countries') - name a country, organisation or study (WHO, Harvard, Finland).
Introducing new ideas in the conclusion.
Memorised, off-topic sentences or copying the question - paraphrase the topic with synonyms.
Starting every sentence with a linking word, or using 'On the other hand' just to add a point.
Forgetting your own opinion - put it in the introduction AND the conclusion.
Attacking the first view inside Body 1 - present it fairly and explain why people hold it.
Unbalanced paragraphs (one long, one short) - keep both at about 5-6 sentences.
Confusing it with an advantages/disadvantages essay - this type is about two opinions held by people.
tips: 4 paragraphs: Introduction (2-3 sentences), Body 1 (5-6 sentences), Body 2 (5-6 sentences), Conclusion (1-2 sentences).
Approximate word targets: introduction ~45-55, each body paragraph ~100-120, conclusion ~35-45 words.
Task 2 counts about twice as much as Task 1 - never run out of time for it (spend 40 minutes).
Use topic vocabulary from the matching 'Writing Topic' set in the vocabulary trainer (4-5 phrases per essay).
Order matters: the disagreed view first, the agreed view second, so the essay builds towards your opinion.
Reporting verbs: argue, contend, maintain, believe, emphasize, claim, hold the view that.
example: Cars vs bicycles in cities: Intro - 'It is often argued that private vehicles offer the most efficient means of urban transportation, whereas others contend that bicycles represent a superior alternative ... I believe that bicycles are the optimal mode ...' Body 1 = cars (Dubai, Houston); Body 2 = bicycles (Amsterdam).
language: It is often argued that ..., whereas others contend that
On the one hand, many people believe
On the other hand, I agree with the perspective that

title: Task 2: Advantages / disadvantages
summary: Explain the advantages and the disadvantages of something - the same number of each; no need to choose a side.
rule: Same number of advantages and disadvantages, in separate paragraphs.

do: 0–5 min: pick the same number of each (1+1, 2+2)
Intro: paraphrase + name both sides
Body 1: advantages; Body 2: disadvantages
Conclusion: sum up both, no new ideas
avoid: Unequal points or paragraph lengths
Choosing a winner when it isn't asked
Mixing both sides in one paragraph
remember: No opinion needed; if any, conclusion only

steps: Minutes 0-5: read the instruction line and identify the essay type; underline every part of the question; choose your position (if needed) and plan two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, explanation, result and a named real-world example. Choose the SAME number of advantages and disadvantages (1+1 or 2+2).

Introduction (2-3 sentences, ~50 words): paraphrase the topic with synonyms and altered structure; thesis naming the advantages and disadvantages you will discuss (While this practice offers clear advantages, such as ..., it also introduces significant drawbacks ...).
Body 1 (~110-130 words): the advantages - topic sentence (One prominent merit of ... is its ability to ...), explanation, example.
Body 2 (~110-130 words): the disadvantages - topic sentence (Conversely, ... / However, the widespread adoption of ... is not without drawbacks.), explanation of how it affects people, example.
Conclusion (1-2 sentences, ~40 words): summarise the core advantage and disadvantage (In conclusion, while ... can serve as a catalyst for ..., it simultaneously ...).

Minutes 35-40: check that every part of the question is answered, your position is the same in the introduction and conclusion, and check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, plurals, spelling of topic words and the word count (250+; aim 280-320).
traps: Under 250 words - the teacher's models are 300-350 words; aim for about 280-320.
Body paragraphs with no named example ('some countries') - name a country, organisation or study (WHO, Harvard, Finland).
Introducing new ideas in the conclusion.
Memorised, off-topic sentences or copying the question - paraphrase the topic with synonyms.
Starting every sentence with a linking word, or using 'On the other hand' just to add a point.

title: Task 2: Problem / solution (and cause / solution)
summary: Explain the problems (or the causes) of a situation and propose solutions - two questions answered in two body paragraphs.

steps: Minutes 0-5: read the instruction line and identify the essay type; underline every part of the question; choose your position (if needed) and plan two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, explanation, result and a named real-world example. Check the first question: 'What problems...?' -> problem paragraph; 'Why / What are the causes...?' -> cause paragraph (cause/solution plan).

Introduction (2 sentences, ~50 words): Sentence 1 paraphrase the topic; Sentence 2 thesis naming the main problem (or cause) and the main solution. Cause/solution template: 'This essay will examine how [cause 1] and [cause 2] cause this problem, and explain why government action is the most realistic solution to this global issue.'

Body 1 (~110-130 words): THE PROBLEM / CAUSE - Sentence 1 topic sentence (The primary reason why ... is ... / The main result of ... is ...); Sentences 2-3 explanation (When ..., ... This means that ...); Sentence 4 result; Sentence 5 real-world example naming a country or organisation (For instance, reports from the WWF show that ...).

Body 2 (~110-130 words): THE SOLUTION - Sentence 1 topic sentence (The primary solution is for governments to ...); Sentences 2-3 how it works and WHO implements it; Sentence 4 the positive result; Sentence 5 a matching example of a country where the solution worked (... Eventually, ... dropped significantly).

Conclusion (1 sentence, ~35-45 words): summarise the main problem/cause and the main solution (In conclusion, a combination of ... and ... causes ... However, this issue can be solved if governments ...).

Introducing new ideas in the conclusion.

Starting every sentence with a linking word, or using 'On the other hand' just to add a point.
Solutions that do not match the problems/causes (each solution should answer one cause: no jobs -> create jobs; low pay -> raise salaries).

steps: Minutes 0-5: read the instruction line and identify the essay type; underline every part of the question; choose your position (if needed) and plan two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, explanation, result and a named real-world example. Decide which side wins: the stronger side gets two points, the weaker side one point.

Introduction (2 sentences, ~50 words): paraphrase; thesis stating which one outweighs the other (I firmly believe that the drawbacks of this practice, specifically regarding ... and ..., far outweigh the single advantage of ...).
Body 1 (~150 words): the STRONGER side - topic sentence, why it is strong, example; then a second topic sentence (Furthermore, / Additionally, ...), why it is strong, example.
Body 2 (~80-90 words): the WEAKER side - topic sentence (On the other hand, ... can serve as ...), why it is NOT strong (However, this benefit is weak because ...), example.
Conclusion (1-2 sentences, ~45 words): summarise and restate which side outweighs (... mean that the disadvantages clearly outweigh the advantages / this disadvantage is heavily eclipsed by ...).

Minutes 35-40: check that every part of the question is answered, your position is the same in the introduction and conclusion, and check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, plurals, spelling of topic words and the word count (250+; aim 280-320).

Body paragraphs with no named example ('some countries') - name a country, organisation or study (WHO, Harvard, Finland).
Introducing new ideas in the conclusion.
Memorised, off-topic sentences or copying the question - paraphrase the topic with synonyms.
Starting every sentence with a linking word, or using 'On the other hand' just to add a point.
Not answering the question directly - say which side outweighs in the introduction AND the conclusion.
Writing a balanced advantages/disadvantages essay with no winner.
Listing the weaker side without limiting it - admit the point, then explain why it is weak.

steps: Minutes 0-5: read the instruction line and identify the essay type; underline every part of the question; choose your position (if needed) and plan two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, explanation, result and a named real-world example. Decide: completely positive or completely negative, and pick two reasons.

Introduction (2-3 sentences, ~50 words): paraphrase the trend (The growing trend of ... represents a major shift ...); thesis clearly stating a completely positive or completely negative development with two reasons (I completely agree that this change is an entirely positive development because it ... and ...).

Body 1 (5-6 sentences, ~110 words): topic sentence with the first reason (First, ...); explanation; example (For instance, data from the ... confirms that ...); result/consequence summarising the ultimate impact.
Body 2 (5-6 sentences, ~110 words): topic sentence with the second reason (Second, ...) - or the opposing side if you chose a balanced view; explanation; example; result/consequence.
Conclusion (1-2 sentences, ~45 words): restate the main points (In conclusion, the transition toward ... is a thoroughly beneficial change for ...).

Minutes 35-40: check that every part of the question is answered, your position is the same in the introduction and conclusion, and check articles (a/an/the), subject-verb agreement, plurals, spelling of topic words and the word count (250+; aim 280-320).

Body paragraphs with no named example ('some countries') - name a country, organisation or study (WHO, Harvard, Finland).
Introducing new ideas in the conclusion.
Memorised, off-topic sentences or copying the question - paraphrase the topic with synonyms.
Starting every sentence with a linking word, or using 'On the other hand' just to add a point.
Not saying clearly whether it is positive or negative.
Explaining the causes of the trend when the question does not ask 'why' (if it does, it is a direct-question essay).
